title: Reading: long passages
lines: ## What you see on screen

A long passage runs about 330 to 450 words, usually in two to four paragraphs, and it comes with three questions. The passage sits on one side of the screen and you may need to scroll it; the questions appear one at a time beside it. As with short passages, you will meet single-answer multiple choice, select all that apply (three choices, one to three correct), and select in passage (click a sentence).
Long passages are less common than short ones, but they reward a clear method more than any other question type, because a reader without a plan gets lost in the details.
## Read for structure, not for detail
You cannot remember every fact in 400 words, and you do not need to. The questions will send you back to the passage. Your first read should answer four questions:
- What is the main point of the whole passage?
- What does each paragraph do?
- Whose views appear, and how do they differ?
- Where does the author stand?

Make a paragraph map: one short note per paragraph, a few words each. On the test, you can jot it on your scratch paper (or the whiteboard if you test at home); in the app, say it to yourself. Spend about two to three minutes on this first read.
## Contrasting views
Long passages often present two or more positions: a traditional view and a challenge to it, two rival theories, or a claim followed by objections. Keep track of who says what. Signal phrases help:
- Introducing someone else's view: some scholars hold, it has long been assumed, according to one account, critics contend.
- Introducing the author's view: however, in fact, a more plausible explanation, this overlooks, it seems clear.
- Conceding a point: admittedly, to be sure, granted, while it is true that.

! The most common error on long passages is attributing a view to the wrong person. If a question asks what the author believes, make sure you are not quoting a view the author describes in order to reject it.
## A sample passage

> Over the past thousand years, many languages have shed the case endings that once marked a noun's role in a sentence, relying instead on word order and small function words. Linguists have long debated why. One school attributes the change chiefly to contact between populations. When adults learn a language as a second tongue, they tend to simplify its least predictable features, and complex systems of endings are notoriously hard for adult learners to master. On this view, languages spoken across trading networks or by mixed communities should lose their endings fastest.

> A second school regards contact as an accelerant rather than a cause. Its proponents point out that sound changes within a language, such as the weakening of unstressed final syllables, can erode endings even in isolated communities. Once two endings come to sound alike, speakers must rely on word order to tell subject from object, and the remaining endings become less useful and more easily lost.

> The two accounts are less opposed than their advocates sometimes suggest. Sound change may supply the initial erosion, while contact determines how quickly the erosion spreads and whether lost distinctions are rebuilt. What neither account yet explains is why some languages with extensive contact, and with plenty of weakened syllables, have kept their endings for centuries. Answering that question will probably require attention to factors, such as the prestige of written standards, that both schools have so far treated as marginal.

> Paragraph map. P1: the puzzle (loss of case endings) and view A (contact with adult learners causes it). P2: view B (internal sound change causes it; contact only speeds it up). P3: the author's view: the two can be combined, but both leave a puzzle unsolved, and a third factor may matter.
> Author's stance: reconciling and gently critical of both schools. Tone: measured, scholarly.
## Question types and how to approach each

- Primary purpose: Match the whole map. Here, "to present two explanations of a linguistic change, suggest how they might be combined, and identify a question both leave open". A choice such as "to defend the contact explanation against its critics" fits only part of P1.

- Structure and function of a paragraph: Ask what the paragraph does relative to the others. P2 "presents an alternative account that reinterprets a factor emphasized in the first paragraph", because it turns contact from a cause into an accelerant.

- Detail: Locate the line first. Question: according to the second school, why do remaining endings become easier to lose? Answer in P2: once some endings sound alike, word order takes over and the others become less useful.

- Inference: Choose what must be true. You can infer that the author considers it possible that written standards help explain why some languages kept their endings, because P3 names them as a factor worth attention in exactly those cases. You cannot infer that the author considers contact unimportant.

- Contrasting views: A question may ask on which point the two schools would agree. Both accept that contact has some effect (school A says it causes the change, school B says it speeds it up), so "contact can influence the rate at which endings are lost" is common ground.
- Author's attitude: Toward the two schools, the author is "appreciative but finds both incomplete". "Dismissive" is too strong; "neutral" ignores the criticism in P3.
## Select all that apply on a long passage
> Question: The passage suggests which of the following about languages spoken by mixed communities? Select all that apply.
> A. View A predicts they will lose case endings relatively quickly.
> B. View B holds that contact alone cannot explain their loss of endings.
> C. They always lose their endings faster than isolated languages.

> A is supported by the last sentence of P1. B is supported by P2, which calls contact an accelerant, not a cause. C is too extreme, and P3 actually mentions languages with extensive contact that kept their endings. Answer: A and B.
## Select in passage on a long passage

On long passages, select-in-passage questions are usually limited to one paragraph; the question tells you which. For example: "Select the sentence in the third paragraph that identifies a limitation shared by both accounts." The answer is the sentence beginning "What neither account yet explains". The next sentence, about written standards, is the trap: it proposes a remedy rather than identifying the limitation.
! Read the question stem word by word. "Identifies a limitation" and "suggests a way to address a limitation" point to different sentences.
## Wrong-answer patterns
The same five patterns as on short passages, but long passages make some of them more tempting:
- Wrong paragraph: a detail that is true but comes from the part of the passage the question is not about.
- Wrong speaker: a view the passage describes, presented as the author's own.
- Too extreme: "proves", "refutes", "entirely", "only" when the author hedges.
- Out of scope: a claim about a topic the passage does not cover, such as which particular languages lost their endings.
- Half right: a choice that describes paragraph 1 correctly and then misstates paragraph 2.
## Timing

Allow about 2 to 3 minutes for the first read and map, then about one minute per question, for a total of roughly 6 to 7 minutes for a passage with three questions. That is within the 1.5 to 2.5 minutes per question that the verbal section allows on average. Do not reread the whole passage for each question; use your map to go straight to the right paragraph.

! If a section opens with a long passage, consider answering the quick text completion and sentence equivalence items first and returning to the passage. You may move freely within a section and change answers until time runs out.
## Quick checklist
- Did I write or say a one-line note for each paragraph?
- Do I know which views belong to which people, and where the author stands?
- Did I find the supporting lines before choosing?
- Did I reject wrong-paragraph and wrong-speaker choices?
